title: Math Camp for Intermediate Microeconomics
text:
Welcome
This mini-book reviews the math you’ll use in Intermediate Microeconomics. Each chapter explains one skill and then gives you unlimited practice: every practice problem is generated with fresh numbers, so you can keep going until the method feels automatic.

title: Math Camp for Intermediate Microeconomics
text:
How the practice problems work

Work each problem on paper first, the same way you will on exams. Then type your final answers to check them.
Answers can be whole numbers, decimals, or fractions (-1/4 and -0.25 both work).
If an answer is wrong, the feedback tries to tell you why, for example if you made a common sign or algebra mistake.
Show solution reveals a worked solution with the same numbers as your problem. Compare it with your own steps.
Every problem has a number. If you get stuck, note the number (for example, Problem #4821) and bring it to office hours: the same number always produces the same problem.

The first time you open a chapter with practice problems, your browser downloads a small version of R, which can take a few seconds. After that, problems load quickly.

title: 1  Solving for Price: Inverse Demand
text:
1.1 The method
Demand curves are usually written with quantity as a function of price, such as \(Q = 120 - 4P\). But graphs in economics put price on the vertical axis, and many problems ask “what price clears the market if \(Q\) units are sold?” For both reasons you’ll often need the inverse demand curve: the same relationship solved for \(P\).
Start from \(Q = a - bP\) and isolate \(P\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
bP &= a - Q \\
P &= \frac{a}{b} - \frac{1}{b}\,Q
\end{aligned}
\]
So the inverse demand curve has intercept \(a/b\) and slope \(-1/b\).

title: 1  Solving for Price: Inverse Demand
text:
NoteExample



If \(Q = 120 - 4P\), then \(4P = 120 - Q\), so \(P = 30 - 0.25Q\). The intercept, 30, is the choke price: the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.








WarningCommon mistake



The slope of the inverse demand curve is \(-1/b\), not \(-b\). Solving for \(P\) means dividing everything by \(b\), including the coefficient on \(Q\).
